lesson.title: dachte & the Suppletive Irregulars
lesson.subtitle: think/thought ↔ denken/dachte, bring/brought ↔ bringen/brachte, go/went ↔ gehen/ging

hook.title: The Verbs That Changed Their Past
hook.content: Some verbs refused the vowel melody and hired a whole new past. English: think, thought. bring, brought. go, went (went is actually a stolen piece of the verb 'wend'!). German did the same, with the same verbs: denken, dachte. bringen, brachte. gehen, ging. And the twist that proves the siblinghood: the borrowed pasts are also cognates — thought and dachte are one word (th→d and the gh→ch you know from Nacht), brought and brachte are one word. Even the irregulars are twins.

footnotes.title: Went Is a Word Thief
footnotes.content: Old English had ēode for the past of 'go'. Middle English replaced it with wente — the past of wend ('to wend one's way'). German ging kept a melody of its own instead. Suppletion — borrowing a past from a neighbor verb — happened independently, but bringen/brachte ↔ bring/brought shows both languages drew from the same ancestral deck.

pattern.title: The Mixed Verbs
pattern.content: denken, dachte, gedacht ↔ think, thought: the vowel changes AND a t arrives — a hybrid of strong and weak. bringen, brachte, gebracht ↔ bring, brought: the same hybrid, the same English twin. danken (to thank) follows its cousin denken: dankte, gedankt. gehen, ging, gegangen ↔ go, went: here German stayed melodic while English went shopping. The pattern to internalize: a handful of high-frequency verbs are 'mixed' — vowel change plus a dental -t- — and English has the identical handful: think, bring, buy, catch, teach.
pattern.linguist_note: thought ↔ dachte is a triple-shift showpiece: th → d, the vowel drift, and gh → ch (the same gh that lives in Nacht and Licht). Every consonant and vowel in the pair obeys a law already in your ledger.

exercises.prompt: Match the mixed verbs with their English twins:
exercises.target_answer: denken / dachte, bringen / brachte, gehen / ging, danken / dankte
exercises.meaning: the think, bring, go, thank pasts
exercises.explanation: The mixed verbs — vowel change plus a dental -t- — exist identically in both languages.

exercises.prompt: Which shifts connect English 'thought' and German 'dachte'?
options: TH → D and GH → CH — plus the vowel drift
exercises.target_answer: TH → D and GH → CH — plus the vowel drift
exercises.explanation: The same machinery as brother/Bruder and Nacht/night, applied to an irregular past. Even the exceptions obey the laws. The ablaut shelf holds the rest: fallen fiel, springen sprang, blasen blies, frieren fror — five verbs, five vowels, one system.

exercises.prompt: Ich-form past of 'denken': 'Ich _____ an dich.' (I thought of you):
exercises.meaning: Ich dachte an dich = I thought of you
exercises.explanation: denken, dachte, gedacht — vowel + dental, exactly like think, thought. treten kept it simpler: trat — tread/trod.

exercises.prompt: What English verb is the twin of 'stehlen'?
exercises.explanation: stehlen/steal — the same ancient theft, with the same strong past: stahl ↔ stole. Both languages kept the loot.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German sentence for 'I brought bread and thought of you':
exercises.target_answer: Ich brachte Brot und dachte an dich
exercises.meaning: I brought bread and thought of you

vocab_hints.note: denken an — the pairing you have used since the TH→D lesson

exercises.explanation: Two mixed pasts in one sentence: brachte and dachte — brought and thought, twins at work.

summary.outcome: Use dachte, brachte, ging — and hear thought and dachte as one double-shift word.

use_example.german: Ich brachte Brot und dachte an dich.
use_example.english: I brought bread and thought of you.

summary.takeaway: The mixed verbs change vowel AND add -t: denken/dachte ↔ think/thought — irregulars, but still twins.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: hatte & war — the fortress pasts of haben and sein, the storyteller's tense.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We think here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir denken heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in dachte & the Suppletive Irregulars.

denken.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Shares the exact vowel-shift relationship with "danken" that English has in "think" and "thank" (a thank is a good thought).

bringen.etymology_derivation: Shared ancient Germanic mixed verb (bring/brought ↔ bringen/gebracht).

danken.etymology_derivation: Danke is an ellipsis of "[Ich] danke [dir/Ihnen]".

schlagen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *slahaną — English slay (Old English slēan) and slog are documented cognates; strong verb: schlug, geschlagen. [wiktionary]

stehlen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stelana, the same root as English steal; both keep the class-4 ablaut — steal, stole, stolen mirrors stehlen, stahl, gestohlen. [wiktionary]

blasen.context_translation: The wind is blowing hard today.
blasen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *blāsan, a class 7 strong verb (blies, geblasen); the fetched page gives no English cognate, but the standard twin is English blow (blew, blown). [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

frieren.context_translation: Are you cold? I am making tea.
frieren.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *freusaną — the page names English freeze as a cognate; the strong past fror, gefroren mirrors froze, frozen. The German infinitive r spread from the old past forms. [wiktionary]

fallen.context_phrase: Das Glas ist vom Tisch gefallen.
fallen.context_translation: The glass fell off the table.
fallen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fallaną; the page lists English fall among the akin forms — a class 7 strong verb on both sides: fell and fiel, fallen and gefallen. [wiktionary]

springen.context_phrase: Das Kind springt über den Bach.
springen.context_translation: The child jumps over the brook.
springen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *springaną (PIE *sprenǵʰ-) — English spring is the documented cognate; strong verb: sprang, gesprungen. [wiktionary]

treten.context_translation: Do not step in the puddle.
treten.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *trudaną — English tread is the documented cognate; the same class 5 ablaut: tritt, trat ↔ tread, trod. [wiktionary]

stoff.context_phrase: Dieser Stoff ist weich und billig.
stoff.context_translation: This fabric is soft and cheap.
stoff.etymology_derivation: Borrowed via Dutch from Old French estoffe - the same French word that gave English stuff; a Germanic root (stopfen) that traveled through French and came back. [wiktionary][etymonline]

sondern.context_phrase: Das ist nicht mein Buch, sondern deins.
sondern.context_translation: That is not my book but yours.
sondern.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *sundraz (apart); the page names English sunder as a straight cognate — nicht X, sondern Y means not X but rather Y. [wiktionary]

stiefmutter.etymology_derivation: stief- (step-) + Mutter, twin of English stepmother; the stief-/step- prefix pair is the same *steupa- root verified under Stiefvater. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
